key_facts: Meta has faced a series of legal actions over allegedly addictive product design for young users, including a $6m jury verdict in March (California), a $942m fine in New Mexico (the first state to win a child-safety lawsuit against Meta), and an $18bn settlement with 48 US states, DC and three territories, under which Meta denied wrongdoing and agreed to two-hour daily time limits for young users and other changes.

key_facts: The ICO had more than 3,600 complaints about automated 'robo calls' in September, a five-year high and nearly three times the July figure; the ICO suspects millions of people receive these calls.

The UK government promised last November that call spoofing would be eliminated within a year; a Home Office spokesman said the Telecommunications Charter is to be delivered by November.

key_facts: Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs in August after disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes; other companies have also exited, and the move is seen by some in the industry as a death knell for solar tiles and by others as an opportunity.

A solar roof might cost twice as much as a rooftop solar panel system before repair costs are factored in; solar roofs are also less efficient due to smaller tiles and reduced airflow that causes heat losses, and coloured tiles are even less efficient.

Freesuns (Swiss) reports sales growth of 20-30% since its 2019 founding; solar roof installations involve more complex engineering, collaboration among roofers, installers and electricians, and more complex building regulations, which add time and cost.

Matrix shingling technology, which connects cut cell strips with conductive adhesive instead of metal wires, can keep current flowing around shaded areas and improves appearance, and is being adopted by Freesuns.

key_facts: The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reported that U.S. families' ability to stay current on debts worsened over the past three years, with debt delinquency at levels not seen since the 2010 survey.

The share of families behind on loan payments at end-2025 rose from about 12% in the prior survey to nearly 20% (a gain of roughly 67%); families two or more months behind rose to more than 8% from 5% in 2022.

Families with payment-to-income ratios above 40% rose to 8.6% from 6.5% in 2022, the highest since 2013. Real median family income rose 7% while average income fell 6%; inflation-adjusted average net worth rose 7% to $1.24 million, and median net worth rose 2% to $215,900.
importance_reason: Official Fed survey showing debt delinquency at its highest since the post-2008 period, a systemic consumer-credit signal.
market_link: Rising household delinquency may weigh on consumer credit performance, bank loan-loss expectations, and consumer spending, with possible implications for rate-policy debates.

key_facts: Prime Minister Andy Burnham promised to curb companies' use of non-compete clauses in employment contracts, saying their use had "gone too far" and was holding back innovative UK companies, including by forcing workers to go without pay after leaving a role and making it harder for growing firms to hire.

Research cited by the government estimates around 5 million jobs in Britain are covered by non-compete clauses, typically lasting around six months; the government has explored a total ban, a ban above a certain salary threshold, or limits on duration.

Burnham said the government will press ahead with new legislation so non-compete clauses can "no longer be a barrier" to hiring; details are expected alongside the Budget on 28 October, and the Recruitment and Employment Confederation warned against "sweeping" changes.
The previous Conservative government had ruled out a total ban after employers warned it could reduce investor confidence or prompt tighter internal information sharing.
importance_reason: Structural labour-market regulation change with a confirmed legislative intent, but scope and details are not yet specified and the timing is pending the Budget.
market_link: Possible effects on UK hiring, start-up and scale-up activity, and investor sentiment toward UK firms; direct market impact is unclear until the scope of restrictions is published.

key_facts: The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader jailed in 2018 for manipulating Euribor.
Five former Barclays bankers' convictions in the rate rigging trials were overturned earlier in the week; Peter Johnson remains convicted and has applied to appeal.
In July 2025 the UK Supreme Court held that the judges in the rate rigging trials had misdirected juries, making whether requests were right or wrong a question of fact for the jury.
Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine trials; eighteen of these convictions have now been acquitted, and all US convictions were overturned in 2022.
importance_reason: Значимое судебное решение по скандалу Libor/Euribor с последствиями для банковского регулирования, но не влияет напрямую на текущие рыночные уровни ставок.

key_facts: Anthropic announced it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour toward its AI, updating its usage policy to let Claude end interactions where people are "cruel"; the company said it had done this in "rare" cases before.

The policy will apply only in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse and will not cover "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research"; what counts as "abusive or cruel behaviour" remains unclear.

The annual usage policy update also forbids using Claude for "deceptive campaigns" and clarifies it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections" ahead of the US midterms, and Anthropic said the previous policy had prevented tools being used to develop weapons.
The changes were first reported by The Verge; the abuse-ban update has drawn social media debate, with critics such as Dr Barry Scannell calling AI anthropomorphisation harmful.
importance_reason: Policy change at a major AI company with reputational and debate value, but no direct market or macro impact.

key_facts: Three former OpenAI researchers (Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang) say they were fired for allegedly mishandling sensitive information, but claim the real reason was raising AI safety concerns. They say they were safety or alignment employees until recently.

OpenAI says its investigation 'confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures' and states the decisions 'were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out'. It describes a 'significant breach of trust' and says it stands by the dismissals.

The former employees published an open letter to OpenAI leadership arguing that their firings made staff 'afraid to speak and operate' in ways that had been integral to working at the company. Korbak says he had raised concerns that the company was losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think.
OpenAI says it is finalising contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks.
importance_reason: Corporate HR/governance dispute at a major AI firm with AI-safety angle; limited direct market impact.
